data.text/html:
Bayes' theorem, the geometry of changing beliefs

An interactive companion to 3Blue1Brown's video. Evidence should not determine your beliefs; it should update them.Colour language used throughout
colour meaning
■ blue the hypothesis ||(H||) (Steve is a librarian)
■ green not the hypothesis ||(\neg H||) (Steve is a farmer)
■ amber people / area that fit the evidence ||(E||) ("meek and tidy soul")
■ red the posterior ||(P(H\mid E)||), the number we want
(The neighbouring bayesian_statistics.py notebook covers Bayesian regression. This one stays with the basic picture: one hypothesis, one piece of evidence, one square.)

data.text/markdown:
0 · Meet Steve

Steve is very shy and withdrawn, invariably helpful but with very little interest in people or the world of reality. A meek and tidy soul, he has a need for order and structure, and a passion for detail.
This description comes from a study by Kahneman and Tversky. Commit to a guess before you scroll on.

data.text/html: <marimo-ui-element object-id='bkHC-0' random-id='f277ccb4-5899-bf1e-b5b3-a64e450dbe75'><marimo-slider data-initial-value='50' data-label='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003eHow likely is it (in %) that Steve is a \u003cstrong\u003elibrarian\u003c/strong\u003e rather than a farmer?\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-start='0' data-stop='100' data-step='1' data-steps='[]' data-debounce='false' data-disabled='false' data-orientation='"horizontal"' data-show-value='true' data-include-input='false' data-full-width='true'></marimo-slider></marimo-ui-element>

<marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003eYou said \u003cstrong\u003e50%\u003c/strong\u003e. Most people say the librarian is more likely, because the description matches the stereotype. Keep your number in mind. Section 1 works out the answer under the video's assumptions.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
1 · Think with a representative sample

Kahneman and Tversky's point is not about whether your stereotypes are right. It is that almost nobody thinks about how many farmers there are compared with librarians. In their paper that ratio was about 20 : 1. The video's recipe:
  1. Picture a representative sample: 10 librarians and 200 farmers.
  2. Your gut says 40% of librarians fit the description and 10% of farmers do.
  3. That gives 4 librarians and 20 farmers who fit, so ||(P(\text{librarian}\mid\text{description}) = \frac{4}{4+20} = 16.7\%||).
Use the sliders, then press 👁 hear the description inside the widget. Evidence restricts the space of possibilities: everyone who doesn't fit fades out.

<marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eKeep the defaults (10 vs 200, 40% vs 10%). A librarian is \u003cstrong\u003e4× as likely\u003c/strong\u003e to fit the description, yet the answer is only \u003cstrong\u003e16.7%\u003c/strong\u003e. There are just too many farmers.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003ePush \u003cem\u003e% of librarians who fit\u003c/em\u003e to \u003cstrong\u003e100%\u003c/strong\u003e. Can the librarian answer get past 50% while farmers outnumber librarians 20 : 1 and 10% of them fit?\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSet both percentages equal. The \"after\" number matches the \"before\" number: \u003cstrong\u003eevidence that fits everyone equally changes nothing.\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"warn"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
2 · From counts to a formula

Generalize: a hypothesis ||(H||) ("Steve is a librarian") and some evidence ||(E||) (the description). We want ||(P(H\mid E)||). The bar means given that: restrict your view to the cases where the evidence holds.
name symbol Steve example
prior ||(P(H)||) ||(1/21||), the share of librarians
likelihood ||(P(E\mid H)||) 40% of librarians fit
(other likelihood) ||(P(E\mid \neg H)||) 10% of farmers fit
posterior ||(P(H\mid E)||) what we want
Counting with a sample of size ||(N||) (the video uses 210), then cancelling ||(N||), gives: ||[ P(H\mid E) \;=\; \frac{N\,P(H)\,P(E\mid H)}{N\,P(H)\,P(E\mid H) \;+\; N\,P(\neg H)\,P(E\mid \neg H)} \;=\; \frac{P(H)\,P(E\mid H)}{P(E)} ||]The sample size ||(N||) was an arbitrary choice, so it has to cancel. Pick any ||(N||) below and watch the counts change while the posterior stays the same.

data.text/markdown: Using the Section 1 sliders: ||(P(H) = 0.0476||), ||(P(E\mid H) = 0.40||), ||(P(E\mid\neg H) = 0.10||). ||[ P(H\mid E) = \frac{\color{#3b82f6}{210}\cdot0.0476\cdot0.40}{\color{#3b82f6}{210}\cdot0.0476\cdot0.40 + \color{#16a34a}{210}\cdot0.9524\cdot0.10} = \frac{4.0}{4.0 + 20.0} = \color{#e4572e}{\mathbf{0.1667}} ||]||(P(E)||), the total share of people who fit the description, is ||((4.0 + 20.0)/210 = 0.1143||).

The counts grow, the red posterior \u003cstrong\u003edoesn't move\u003c/strong\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eAt \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(N = 210||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e with the defaults you should read exactly \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(4/(4+20)||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eThe denominator \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(P(E)||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e is almost never known directly. You \u003cstrong\u003ecompute\u003c/strong\u003e it by splitting into \"\u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(H||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e true\" and \"\u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(H||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e false\". That split is the second term.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"warn"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
3 · The picture to keep in your head: probability as area

The video's advice: don't memorize the formula, draw this diagram. Replace the 210 people with a 1 × 1 square of all possibilities. Probability is area.
  • The left strip, width ||(P(H)||), holds the librarians. The right strip, width ||(P(\neg H)||), holds the farmers.
  • In each strip, the amber bottom part is where the evidence holds. Its height is the likelihood: ||(P(E\mid H)||) on the left, ||(P(E\mid\neg H)||) on the right.
  • The left amber rectangle has area ||(P(H)\,P(E\mid H) = P(H \cap E)||).
Seeing the evidence throws away everything that isn't amber. The posterior is the share of the remaining amber area that is blue: ||[P(H\mid E) = \frac{\text{left amber area}}{\text{total amber area}}||]Drag the vertical divider (prior) and the tops of the two amber bars (likelihoods). Toggle restrict to evidence to see the uneven, "wonky" shape that is left.

It doesn't replace it.\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"warn"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
4 · Why "40 out of 100" beats "40%": Linda

In another Kahneman and Tversky experiment, people read about Linda: 31, single, outspoken, very bright, majored in philosophy, concerned with discrimination and social justice, joined anti-nuclear demonstrations. Then they were asked which is more likely:
  1. Linda is a bank teller.
  2. Linda is a bank teller and is active in the feminist movement.
85% chose (2). But feminist bank tellers are a subset of bank tellers, so (2) can never be more likely than (1). When the question was reframed as "of 100 people who fit this description, how many are…", the error dropped to 0%. Try it both ways.

data.text/markdown:
5 · Unfinished business: who is Steve?

Some psychologists dispute the "irrational" verdict. Who is Steve? A random American? A friend of the psychologists? Someone you are likely to meet? (Grant says he runs into many more librarians than farmers.) How likely each group is to fit the description is also open to interpretation. The diagram absorbs the whole debate:
  • arguments about context move the prior (the divider),
  • arguments about personalities and stereotypes move the likelihoods (the amber bars).
Choose a framing for Steve and set the likelihoods. The heat map shows the posterior for every prior × likelihood ratio, and the ★ marks your current choice.

With the same stereotypes, Steve is now \u003cstrong\u003e80%\u003c/strong\u003e likely to be a librarian. The context argument is entirely an argument about the prior.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eUnder the \u003cem\u003eModern US stats\u003c/em\u003e prior, how big does the likelihood ratio have to be to reach 50%? (Find the dashed line: the ratio has to equal the prior odds against.)\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eContours run \u003cstrong\u003ediagonally\u003c/strong\u003e: doubling the prior odds and doubling the likelihood ratio have the same effect.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"warn"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
6 · Sandbox: draw your own square

Pick a scenario to load into a fresh square, then drag freely. Below the square, the posterior becomes the new prior: the chart shows what happens if you keep seeing independent pieces of evidence with the same likelihoods. Each update is just a new square that starts from the last posterior.

Recap

idea in the video in this notebook
Base rates matter Steve: 20 farmers per librarian. "Rationality is recognizing which facts are relevant." §1 people grid
Evidence restricts the space Keep only those who fit; 4 of 24 = 16.7% §1 👁 button, §3 restrict toggle
Bayes' theorem ||(P(H\mid E)=\dfrac{P(H)P(E\mid H)}{P(H)P(E\mid H)+P(\neg H)P(E\mid\neg H)}||) §2 live formula, ||(N||) cancels
Prior / likelihood / posterior names for ||(P(H)||), ||(P(E\mid H)||), ||(P(H\mid E)||) §2 table
Probability as area 1 × 1 square; posterior = blue share of the amber region §3 draggable square
Irrelevant evidence equal likelihoods leave the belief unchanged §3, sandbox "pizza"
Counts beat percentages Linda: 85% → 0% errors with "out of 100" §4
The debate fits the diagram context → prior, stereotypes → likelihoods §5 heat map
Beliefs keep updating today's posterior is tomorrow's prior §6 sandbox
Mantra: evidence should not determine beliefs, it should update them.
